clue.text: 'Play late,' he's written in error

indicators.note: something done in error is done wrongly, so the letters of these words are set out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer confesses that he submitted his play past the deadline, owning up to the mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a verb telling someone to perform late, but it is the definition. 'in error' signals the rearrangement of all fourteen letters of LATE HE'S WRITTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare wrote this late romance, one of his stage works, so it is an example of a drama.

clue.text: Scarlett's place is housing this person's crowns

indicators.note: one thing housing another holds it inside, so the setter's self-reference goes within the house's name

parts.note: Tara is the plantation home of Scarlett O'Hara in Gone with the Wind
the setter speaking of themself, I
's is the short form of is

explanation.surface: Scarlett O'Hara's mansion is said to hold the speaker's collection of royal headgear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'housing' puts I inside TARA'S, read as TARA + S for 'place is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental headband, a kind of small coronet worn on formal occasions.

clue.text: Use 75% of polymers wrongly

indicators.note: placed wrongly means the remaining letters are set out in another order
polymers has eight letters, and three quarters of it is its first six, so the final pair is dropped

explanation.surface: A chemistry instruction about misusing most of a batch of plastics.
explanation.walkthrough: '75% of' trims POLYMERS to POLYME, and 'wrongly' rearranges those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To make use of something is to put it to work, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Sorry round with bogey pair unravelled

indicators.note: something unravelled has come apart, so these letters are pulled apart and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A golfer apologises after a round undone by two bogeys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins ROUND to BOGEY PAIR, and 'unravelled' rearranges all fourteen letters. A bogey is one over par on a golf hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are polite set phrases for apologising or for asking someone to repeat what they said.

clue.text: 12 and offensive

definitions.meaning: refers to 12 across, meaning dull or bland, as food lacking flavour is
in poor taste, likely to upset people

explanation.definitionFit: Lacking flavour gives the bland sense; lacking good judgement gives the crude, offensive one.

clue.text: Wind section's leader dances

parts.note: to wind thread or line is to reel it in

indicators.note: a section's leader is the word's opening letter

explanation.surface: The front player of an orchestra's woodwind section takes to the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind section' suggests the orchestra, but Wind is a verb giving REEL, and 'leader' picks the S of section's.
explanation.definitionFit: Reels are lively Scottish and Irish folk dances, so the plural noun names several such dances.

clue.text: See 1
Dislike a particular edition

parts.note: a version is one particular edition or form of something

explanation.surface: Someone takes against one specific printing of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a strong dislike, so the noun is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Writer tries to encapsulate current time

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose, so the word for tries surrounds the electrical symbol

parts.note: essays are attempts, as to essay is to try
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An author attempts to capture the mood of the present moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to encapsulate' puts I inside ESSAYS to give ESSAYIS, then T follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An essayist is an author who writes short prose pieces on a theme, so a kind of writer.

clue.text: Meandering hotel tour bores Mr Fixit?

indicators.note: a meandering path wanders about, so these letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A rambling guided tour of a hotel tires its guests.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks Mr Fixit as a playful description rather than a strict synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone called in to diagnose and solve problems is nicknamed Mr Fixit, a person who sorts things out.

clue.text: Enough drink imbibed by politician? Quite the opposite!

indicators.note: read literally, the drink goes inside the politician; taken with the reversal instruction, the politician goes inside the drink
this tells the solver to swap which piece holds which, so the drink contains the politician

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician drinks just enough, or does the drink swallow the politician?
explanation.walkthrough: 'imbibed by' alone would put the drink inside the politician; 'Quite the opposite!' swaps container and contents.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty means more than enough, a fair adjective synonym for sufficient.

clue.text: Reported cut head in Kent town

indicators.note: reported means spoken of, so the solver listens to the words rather than reading them

parts.note: to shear is to cut, and a ness is a headland, together sounding like the answer

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about someone who gashed their head in a Kent town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' is the geographical kind, a ness or headland. Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheerness is a port town on the Isle of Sheppey in the county of Kent.

clue.text: Dull and terribly annoyed

indicators.note: done terribly means done badly, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone who is boring and also very cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Anodyne describes something inoffensive and bland, deliberately avoiding anything stimulating.

clue.text: Soft game with unknown

parts.note: squash is a racket game played in a walled court
Y is an algebraic unknown, as x, y, z are

explanation.surface: A gentle ball game against an unidentified opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: Squashy means easily pressed in, a synonym of yielding or soft to the touch.

clue.text: 101 left in outstanding debts, being arrogant

parts.note: super means excellent or outstanding
CI is 101 in Roman numerals
IOUs are written notes acknowledging debts

explanation.surface: Someone with a hundred and one unpaid debts still behaves haughtily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding debts' reads as unpaid bills, but outstanding works alone as excellent; 'in' places the Roman 101 plus L within the debts. 'being' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Supercilious describes a haughty person who looks down on others, a close synonym.

clue.text: Sure about working if turning up with depression?

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
on means working, as a machine is on

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from the bottom upward, backwards

parts.note: a dent is a small hollow or depression

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you are certain, given you keep working while depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses IF to FI.
explanation.definitionFit: To be confident is to feel certain, so the adjective is a synonym.

clue.text: Fool embracing famous footballer — love is dangerous stuff

indicators.note: one piece embracing another wraps around it, so the fool's letters enclose the footballer and the zero

parts.note: an ass is a foolish person
George Best was a celebrated Northern Ireland and Manchester United footballer
love means nil in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A tabloid line: an idiot hugging a star footballer, and romance proves hazardous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link word. George Best was a famous footballer of the 1960s and 70s.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral whose dust causes lung disease, a notoriously hazardous material.

clue.text: Office worker can start to get seductive

parts.note: a temp is a temporary office worker
a tin is a can

indicators.note: the start to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A temporary office worker can begin to turn alluring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb but is the container, TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tempting is alluring and invites you in, a close synonym.

clue.text: A woolly state … or an embarrassed one?

definitions.meaning: playfully, the condition of being like a sheep, a woolly animal
a state of looking awkward and abashed

explanation.definitionFit: Read whimsically, the word means being sheep-like; in its real sense it means awkward embarrassment.

clue.text: Brown little bear eats girl

indicators.note: one thing eating another takes it inside, so the bear's name holds the girl's

parts.note: Ted is short for teddy, a toy bear
Ann is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A cartoonish horror: a small brown bear devours a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' looks like the bear's colour, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanned skin has been browned by the sun, so the adjective fits.

clue.text: Always in London area? Harsh!

indicators.note: one piece in another sits inside it, so the word for always goes within the area abbreviation

parts.note: SE is a London postcode area, South East
ever means always, as in for ever

explanation.surface: A complaint that life in one corner of London is permanently tough.
explanation.walkthrough: SE is the London postal district for the south-east of the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe treatment is strict and unsparing, a direct adjective synonym.

clue.text: Space for a gold sovereign?

parts.note: an em is a printer's space, as wide as the letter M
per means for each, for a, as in miles per hour
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Somewhere to keep a gold sovereign coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gold sovereign' reads as a coin, but sovereign here means a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the supreme ruler of an empire, a kind of monarch.

clue.text: One might charge money

definitions.meaning: a large horned animal known for charging at threats

explanation.definitionFit: The animal is famous for charging; the slang word for cash dates from the seventeenth century.

clue.text: A region troubled in time long ago

indicators.note: something troubled is disturbed, so these letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A district that was in turmoil in ancient times.
explanation.definitionFit: This prehistoric period followed the Bronze Age, when iron tools came into use.

clue.text: Finally felt upset about obituary for old fossil

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word that follows
one piece about another goes around it, so the word for upset surrounds the death notice

parts.note: to rile someone is to upset them
obit is short for obituary

explanation.surface: A reader was finally upset by an obituary for an elderly bore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old fossil' suggests an old-fashioned person, but here it is a real fossil. 'upset' is not an anagram signal: it gives RILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Trilobites were marine arthropods extinct for 250 million years, now known only from fossils.

clue.text: Possibly perfect form of language

parts.note: the perfect is one example of a verb form expressing time, as are the past and future

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson about flawless speech or writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perfect form' reads as flawless, but perfect is a grammatical term.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar names verb forms for time, and the perfect is one such form, marked by 'possibly' as an example.

clue.text: Give a narrative

parts.note: to give is to bend or yield under weight, as to sag does

explanation.surface: An instruction to tell a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' looks like an instruction but means sag, as a shelf does.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long story, originally a medieval Norse tale of heroes.

clue.text: Pay British bank for pedestrian crossing

parts.note: to foot the bill is to pay it
a ridge is a raised bank of earth

explanation.surface: A demand that a British bank fund a new road crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British bank' reads as a high-street bank, but bank is a ridge of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A footbridge carries walkers over a road, river or railway, a crossing for those on foot.
